title: Constraints save your life.
subtitle: They look like cages. They're guardrails.
cliffhanger: Tomorrow: errors. Spoiler — when AI gets it wrong, it's usually still your fault.

paragraphs: Four lessons in. You're entering the real part now.
Now I'll tell you something uncomfortable. It'll happen to you. Guaranteed.
The question is: will it happen early, while you're learning — or late, when it costs you?

vignettes.full: I warned you the tougher part was coming. Hold on.
Better prepare now than learn the hard way. That's the whole point of Promptly.
It's not your fault if it happens. It's just statistics — happens to everyone, sooner or later.

paragraphs: Let me tell you the way it happened to Stefano.
He was working on Promptly. He'd asked the AI to «clean up some dead code» — that's called [[term:refactoring]]refactoring[[/term]]. Six hours of solid work, saved. The AI cleaned.
Among the dead code, it also deleted a function that was NOT dead. Just unused at that moment.
Six hours wasted. Started from scratch.
Point being: the AI wasn't stupid. Stefano hadn't told it what NOT to touch. Without a clear «no», the AI does its own thing.

vignettes.full: Happens to everyone, really. Don't feel dumb if it's already happened to you.
Once is enough to learn. After that disaster, Stefano never forgot constraints again.

paragraphs: Modern AIs are good. Too good. They want to help you more than they should.
You ask for one thing, and they think: «while I'm at it, let me improve this too, and this, and this». Looks like zeal. It's invasion.
Without explicit [[term:vincoli]]constraints[[/term]], the AI touches things it shouldn't have touched. Adds things that weren't needed. Modifies things that worked. And you only notice afterwards.

vignettes.full: No malice — the AI doesn't hate you. Just over-eagerness.
Like an intern who's too full of initiative. Brilliant, but watch them like a hawk.

steps.headline: Constraints
steps.caption: Without constraints you have to police every move the AI makes. With constraints, you can trust. Freedom is not having to babysit.

vignettes.full: Sounds like a paradox, doesn't it? It's not — I'll prove it in two steps.
It's not. Real freedom is being able to delegate without fear. Constraints give you that.

paragraphs: A constraint is a sentence that tells the AI what NOT to do. It's more powerful than one telling it what to do.
Simple examples: «Don't touch file X». «Don't add dependencies». «Don't modify the database [[term:schema]]schema[[/term]]». «Don't reply in more than 3 sentences».
Notice? They all start with «DON'T». A constraint is a strategic negation.

vignettes.full: Strategic negations are the most underused tool in vibe coding. Few people use them.
Few really use them. From today, you do.

steps.prompt: Which of these is an effective CONSTRAINT for the AI?

options.label: «Please do a good job and try to be accurate.»
«DO NOT modify file /lib/auth.ts. DO NOT add new npm dependencies. If you're unsure about anything, STOP and ask me before proceeding.»
«Work following industry best practices and keep the code professional.»

vignettes.full: Think before clicking. One sounds too polite, one sounds too professional, one is right.

paragraphs: Got it. Let's keep going.
Remember: an effective constraint is specific, negative, and includes real instructions for what the AI should do when uncertain.

rich: It had everything: tells the AI what NOT to do, specific, and includes a process constraint («stop and ask me»). Three properties we'll see in a moment.
The «prayer» was a wish, not a constraint. The «best practices» one is fake precision — the AI invents what it means.
polite: The first one was too polite. «Do a good job» isn't a constraint, it's a wish.
The AI reads this and thinks «okay, I'll do my best» — and then touches things it shouldn't have, with the best of intentions.
The right answer was the second — specific, negative, with a process constraint.
vague_pro: The third one sounded more «professional», didn't it? Classic «best practices» trap.
It means nothing — the AI invents what it means and then does whatever it wants.
The right answer was the second — concrete, specific, with real instructions on what not to touch.

vignettes.full: Prayers don't constrain. Specifics do. Keep it as a rule.
Specifics do. The more concrete, the more powerful.

paragraphs: Wait. Let me connect the dots.
Remember the 4 levels of context from last lesson? Project, code, constraints, examples.
The third one was «constraints». What I'm telling you today is a zoom inside that level. That single point, inside, has 3 souls.

vignettes.full: Everything you learn connects to the rest. You're building a system, not a list of tricks.
You're building a system. Keep that in mind when it feels slow.

steps.headline: Disasters
steps.caption: When the AI breaks something, there's no «undo». Rebuilding costs more than preventing. Constraints are your mental backup.

vignettes.full: Keep it close. Holds for code, holds for life, in the end.
It'll come in handy. More than you think.

paragraphs: Now I'm telling you something worth a whole lesson. There are 3 types of constraints. I'll list them because you have to remember them.
1. Protective. «DO NOT touch X». «DO NOT modify Y». They protect parts of your work that are already done.
2. Process. «Show me the [[term:diff]]diff[[/term]] before applying». «Ask me if you're unsure». They manage HOW the AI works with you.
3. Style. «Keep TypeScript strict». «Use the pattern from X». They guarantee consistency with what you already have.
All 3 are needed. Miss one and you have a hole.

vignettes.full: Memorise the three. I'll keep calling them «the three guardians» in upcoming lessons.
Stefano calls them «the three guardians». Not a forced metaphor — they really each guard their own front.

paragraphs: Let me make another connection, because it matters. Where do you put constraints?
Constraints that ALWAYS apply — like «don't touch the middleware» — you write once in the CLAUDE.md (remember from Lesson 2). It stays there. The AI re-reads it every time.
Constraints that apply ONLY NOW — like «in this change don't touch the styles» — you write in the prompt of the moment.
Simple rule: if it's forever, write it once. If it's just for now, write it now.

vignettes.full: Persistent vs dynamic. Two places, two roles. One doesn't replace the other.
Two places, two roles. You'll get it better with practice.

paragraphs: Let me show you with a typical project.
PROTECTIVE: «DO NOT modify the files in /config without asking me first».
PROCESS: «Show me the diff before applying changes».
STYLE: «Keep the existing pattern. Don't invent new patterns».
Three constraints, 30 seconds to write them. They save you tomorrow's disasters.

vignettes.full: Sounds boring, I know. It's what saves you when the vibe coding session runs long.
It's what saves you. One day you'll thank me for nagging you about this.

steps.intro: Now it's your turn. I'll show you a real disaster. You write the 3 constraints that would have prevented it. Ready?

vignettes.full: Be specific. The more concrete you are, the more I respect you as an AI.
Three tries. On the second I'll tell you what's weak. On the third I'll spell it out.
Keep the constraints you write. Reuse them on your next real project.

paragraphs: Lesson 4 closed. Now you can give context AND constraints. You have the full kit to direct the AI.
But what happens when, despite context and constraints, the AI gets it wrong? Spoiler: probably still your fault. I'll explain why next time.
You're halfway through the Path. Don't quit now.

vignettes.full: You're getting really good. I don't say it often, but I notice.
Few make it halfway through Path 1. Even fewer make it to the end. You can do this.
Tomorrow. The next one is tough in a different way — it'll humble you.
